# topocast

*coarse climate grids at the resolution of the terrain*

<!-- badges: start -->
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/topocast)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=topocast)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/gcol33/topocast/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/gcol33/topocast/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/gcol33/topocast/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/gcol33/topocast)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
<!-- badges: end -->

```{r downscale, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.3, dpi = 140, fig.alt = "A simulated precipitation field on a 1.2 km grid drawn as coarse blocks, beside the same field downscaled onto a 100 m elevation model, where the terrain texture shows through; both panels share one colour scale"}
library(topocast)
library(terra)

set.seed(1)
fine <- rast(nrows = 180, ncols = 180, xmin = 0, xmax = 18000, ymin = 0, ymax = 18000,
             crs = "EPSG:32632")
xy <- crds(fine)
elev <- setValues(fine, 1300 + 700 * sin(xy[, 1] / 2700) + 500 * cos(xy[, 2] / 2200) +
                          260 * sin(xy[, 1] / 760) + 200 * cos(xy[, 2] / 900))
names(elev) <- "elev"

coarse_prec <- aggregate(elev, fact = 12, fun = "mean")
coarse_prec <- 1100 - 0.24 * coarse_prec +
  setValues(coarse_prec, rnorm(ncell(coarse_prec), 0, 22))
names(coarse_prec) <- "prec"

downscaled <- topocast(prec ~ elev, data = coarse_prec, onto = elev, radius = 5)

rng <- range(c(values(coarse_prec), values(downscaled)), na.rm = TRUE)
pal <- hcl.colors(256, "Spectral")

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.4, 0.5), oma = c(0, 0, 0, 3), bg = "white")
plot(coarse_prec, col = pal, range = rng, axes = FALSE, legend = FALSE, mar = NA,
     main = "coarse precipitation  (1.2 km)")
plot(downscaled, col = pal, range = rng, axes = FALSE, mar = NA,
     main = "downscaled onto terrain  (100 m)")
par(op)
```

topocast downscales a coarse raster, such as a 1 km precipitation grid, to the resolution of a fine predictor, such as a 100 m elevation model.

In a square window around every coarse cell, topocast fits a linear regression of the coarse variable on the coarse predictors. The fitted intercept and slopes are resampled to the fine grid and applied to the fine predictors, so the output carries the structure of the terrain with coefficients that vary across the map. This is the regression step behind high-resolution climate surfaces such as CHELSA (Karger et al. 2017), fitted locally and with any number of named predictors. The window fits use summed-area tables in C++, so a radius of 30 coarse cells costs the same per cell as a radius of 3. You can map the local coefficients and the fit quality, and decide where the downscaled detail is supported by the terrain.

topocast supports:

- **Several predictors.** `prec ~ elev + slope + twi` fits elevation, slope, topographic wetness or any aligned covariate jointly. Layers are matched by name between the coarse and the fine data, so a missing layer is reported by name.
- **Several responses in one call.** `cbind(prec, tmin) ~ elev` downscales variables that share the terrain. The window design is built and factored once and solved against each response.
- **Time series.** A stack of coarse periods passed as `anomaly` is carried onto the downscaled baseline, as a ratio for precipitation or as a difference for temperature.
- **Prediction at points.** Station or plot locations as an `sf` or `SpatVector` object receive a prediction column instead of a grid.
- **Fit quality on the map.** `diagnostics = TRUE` returns grids of the local R², the residual standard deviation and the number of valid cells in each window.
- **Common spatial classes.** terra `SpatRaster`, raster `Raster*` and `stars` grids are accepted, and the result comes back in the class of the fine data.

## Installation

Install the released version from CRAN. Windows and macOS get a binary and need no build tools:

```r
install.packages("topocast")
```

The development version compiles C++ code. Install the build tools for your operating system first:

| Operating system | Build tools |
|---|---|
| Windows | [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/) matching your R version |
| macOS | Run `xcode-select --install` in Terminal |
| Debian / Ubuntu | Install `r-base-dev` |

Check that R can find the compiler:

```r
pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)
```

Then install topocast from GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/topocast")
```

The compiler has to support C++17. The C++ code links R's own LAPACK and BLAS through RcppArmadillo and needs no further system library. On Linux, [terra](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/), which topocast uses for rasters, builds against GDAL, GEOS and PROJ.

### Optional: multithreading

OpenMP lets the window fits use several CPU threads, set by the `threads` argument of [`topocast()`](https://gillescolling.com/topocast/reference/topocast.html) and [`window_regression()`](https://gillescolling.com/topocast/reference/window_regression.html). By default every available core is used.

Rtools on Windows and the default compiler on Linux include OpenMP. Without it, the package installs and fits on one thread with the same results.

#### macOS setup

Apple's compiler needs an additional OpenMP runtime. Install it in Terminal:

```sh
brew install libomp
```

Before installing topocast from source, add the settings for your Mac to `~/.R/Makevars`, R's personal compiler-settings file. Create the directory and file if needed.

**Apple Silicon:**

```makefile
CPPFLAGS += -I/opt/homebrew/opt/libomp/include -Xclang -fopenmp
LDFLAGS += -L/opt/homebrew/opt/libomp/lib -lomp
```

**Intel:**

```makefile
CPPFLAGS += -I/usr/local/opt/libomp/include -Xclang -fopenmp
LDFLAGS += -L/usr/local/opt/libomp/lib -lomp
```

## Usage

1. Give the coarse variable and the fine predictor layer names that the formula uses.
2. Call `topocast()` with the formula, the coarse grid as `data`, the fine grid as `onto` and the window `radius` in coarse cells.
3. Use the result, which lies on the grid of `onto`, or map the local fit with `coefficients = TRUE` or `diagnostics = TRUE`.

The example builds a 100 m elevation model and a 600 m precipitation grid that falls with elevation:

```{r usage}
library(topocast)
library(terra)

set.seed(1)
elev <- rast(nrows = 120, ncols = 120, xmin = 0, xmax = 12000,
             ymin = 0, ymax = 12000, crs = "EPSG:32632")
xy <- crds(elev)
elev <- setValues(elev, 1200 + 600 * sin(xy[, 1] / 2500) +
                          400 * cos(xy[, 2] / 2000))
names(elev) <- "elev"

prec <- 900 - 0.18 * aggregate(elev, fact = 6)
prec <- prec + setValues(prec, rnorm(ncell(prec), 0, 20))
names(prec) <- "prec"

fine_prec <- topocast(prec ~ elev, data = prec, onto = elev, radius = 4)
fine_prec
```

The coarse grid has 20 by 20 cells and the result has the 120 by 120 cells of the elevation model. A radius of 4 gives each regression a window of 9 by 9 coarse cells. Here `data` contains only the precipitation, so the coarse elevation is aggregated from `onto` before the fit.

The coarse `data` is a `SpatRaster`, `Raster*` or `stars` grid, and the layer named on the left of the formula is the response. The fine `onto` is a grid, or a set of points, that carries the predictors named on the right. Both share a coordinate reference system; a mismatch stops the call and names both systems.

## Several predictors, responses and periods

Each predictor named in the formula is fitted jointly, and `cbind()` on the left downscales several responses with one shared design. A stack of coarse periods passed as `anomaly` fits the baseline once and carries each period onto it, with `type = "ratio"` for non-negative variables such as precipitation and `type = "additive"` for temperature. [Getting started with topocast](https://gillescolling.com/topocast/articles/getting-started.html) runs each of these on one landscape, along with points and the other spatial classes.

## Mapping the local fit

`coefficients = TRUE` returns the fitted layer with the intercept and one slope per predictor on the fine grid. The slope of elevation is the local lapse rate:

```{r coefficients}
grids <- topocast(prec ~ elev, data = prec, onto = elev, radius = 4,
                  coefficients = TRUE)
names(grids)
```

`diagnostics = TRUE` adds the local R² (`r.squared`), the residual standard deviation and the count of valid cells in each window. `clamp = TRUE` bounds the output to the observed range of the coarse response where the fine terrain reaches values the window never saw. Averaging the result back to the coarse grid does not reproduce the coarse input exactly, because the coarse residual is not carried.

## How the window regression works

Each window fit needs only sums of the response, the predictors and their products over the window. Summed-area tables give each sum in four lookups, so the cost per cell does not depend on the radius. [How moving-window downscaling works](https://gillescolling.com/topocast/articles/how-it-works.html) derives the method and the masking rules. `window_regression()` runs the same fit on plain numeric matrices, without terra.

## Documentation

Start with [Getting started with topocast](https://gillescolling.com/topocast/articles/getting-started.html): one landscape downscaled with one and several predictors, several responses, a time series and points.

- [How moving-window downscaling works](https://gillescolling.com/topocast/articles/how-it-works.html): the local regression, summed-area tables, masking and fit quality.
- [Full reference](https://gillescolling.com/topocast/reference/): every function.

## Getting help

Questions and bug reports go to the [GitHub issues](https://github.com/gcol33/topocast/issues). A bug report is easiest to act on with a small reproducible example, for instance made with [reprex](https://reprex.tidyverse.org/).

```{r citation, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cit <- citation("topocast")
fence <- function(lang, x) cat("```", lang, "\n", paste(x, collapse = "\n\n"), "\n```\n\n", sep = "")
cat(attr(cit, "mheader"), "\n\n", sep = "")
fence("text", format(cit, style = "text"))
cat("BibTeX:\n\n")
fence("bibtex", format(cit, style = "bibtex"))
```
